title: Mock Exam B — Claude Code & CI/CD
description: Covers Domains 3 and 4 through Scenarios 2 (Claude Code Configuration) and 5 (CI/CD Pipelines)

questions.question: Your team has the following CLAUDE.md files: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (personal), a project-root CLAUDE.md, and a subdirectory src/api/CLAUDE.md. The project-root file says 'Use 4-space indentation' while the subdirectory file says 'Use 2-space indentation for all TypeScript files.' When editing a file in src/api/, which indentation rule applies?

options.A: 4-space indentation, because the project root always takes precedence over subdirectories
options.B: 2-space indentation, because the most specific (nearest) CLAUDE.md wins for files in that directory
options.C: The personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md setting, because user preferences override project settings
options.D: Neither — conflicting rules cancel each other out, so Claude uses its default behavior

explanations.A: WRONG — CLAUDE.md uses a cascade hierarchy where more specific files override more general ones, similar to CSS specificity. The project root is NOT the highest priority for subdirectory files.
explanations.B: CORRECT — The CLAUDE.md cascade is: enterprise policy > project root > subdirectory > personal preferences. For files in src/api/, the src/api/CLAUDE.md is the most specific match and its rules take precedence for files in that directory.
explanations.C: WRONG — Personal preferences (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) have the LOWEST priority in the cascade. They are overridden by all project-level settings. This ensures project conventions are enforced consistently across team members.
explanations.D: WRONG — There is no conflict cancellation. The cascade hierarchy is deterministic: the most specific file wins.

questions.question: You are creating reusable automation for your team. One developer wants a workflow that reads a GitHub issue, creates a branch, implements the fix, and submits a PR. Another wants a quick snippet that formats import statements. Which Claude Code extension mechanism should each use?

options.A: Both should use custom slash commands defined in .claude/commands/
options.B: The multi-step workflow should use a custom slash command; the import formatter should use a skill (via Skill tool)
options.C: Both should use skills for maximum reusability
options.D: The multi-step workflow should be a skill; the import formatter should be a custom slash command since it is simpler

explanations.A: WRONG — Custom slash commands work for both, but skills provide better encapsulation for focused, reusable operations like formatting. Commands are better for multi-step workflows that orchestrate multiple actions.
explanations.B: CORRECT — Commands (defined in .claude/commands/*.md) are ideal for multi-step workflows: they can include detailed instructions, reference files, and orchestrate complex sequences. Skills are better for focused, reusable operations that can be invoked programmatically and composed into larger workflows.
explanations.C: WRONG — Skills are not ideal for complex multi-step workflows. The GitHub issue-to-PR workflow involves reading issues, git branching, code changes, testing, and PR creation — this is better expressed as a command with step-by-step instructions.
explanations.D: WRONG — This is backwards. Skills are for focused reusable operations (like formatting). Commands are for multi-step workflows (like the issue-to-PR pipeline).

questions.question: A junior developer asks: 'Should I always use plan mode before letting Claude make changes?' Which response best reflects the recommended practice?

options.A: Yes, always use plan mode first — it prevents mistakes by forcing Claude to think before acting
options.B: No, never use plan mode — it wastes time because Claude can plan and execute simultaneously
options.C: Use plan mode for complex or risky changes (architectural decisions, large refactors) but skip it for well-understood, small changes (rename a variable, fix a typo)
options.D: Use plan mode only when you disagree with Claude's initial approach

explanations.A: WRONG — Always using plan mode adds unnecessary overhead for simple changes. A typo fix or variable rename doesn't need an architectural plan.
explanations.B: WRONG — Skipping plan mode for complex changes is risky. Claude might take an approach that's technically correct but architecturally wrong, leading to costly rework.
explanations.C: CORRECT — Plan mode is a risk management tool. Use it when: (1) the change is complex or ambiguous, (2) there are multiple valid approaches and you want to choose, (3) the change is irreversible or hard to undo, (4) you're unfamiliar with the codebase area. Skip it for trivial, well-understood changes.
explanations.D: WRONG — By the time you disagree, Claude may have already made changes. Plan mode should be proactive (before changes), not reactive (after seeing unwanted changes).

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline runs Claude Code for automated code review. Currently, all review tasks share a single long-running session to 'save context.' Reviews are occasionally producing recommendations that reference code from DIFFERENT pull requests. What is the root cause and fix?

options.A: The model is hallucinating — add a disclaimer to each review output
options.B: Session bleed: shared sessions accumulate context from prior reviews. Fix: use isolated sessions (--session-id per PR) so each review starts with a clean context
options.C: The context window is too large — reduce max_tokens to limit how far back the model looks
options.D: Add a system prompt saying 'Only reference code from the current pull request'

explanations.A: WRONG — This isn't hallucination (fabricating facts). The model is correctly recalling code — but from the WRONG PR's context. The issue is architectural, not model behavior.
explanations.B: CORRECT — Session bleed is a critical CI/CD anti-pattern. When reviews share a session, context from PR #1 leaks into the review of PR #2. The fix is session isolation: each review gets its own session ID, ensuring a clean context. This is Anti-Pattern #14.
explanations.C: WRONG — max_tokens controls output length, not context scope. Reducing it would truncate the review output, not prevent cross-PR context leakage.
explanations.D: WRONG — Prompt-based enforcement is probabilistic (Anti-Pattern #3). The model might still reference prior context. Session isolation is the deterministic fix.

questions.question: Your team wants to use Claude for bulk migration of 500 configuration files from YAML to TOML format. Each file is independent. The task is not time-sensitive — results are needed by tomorrow morning. Which execution strategy is most cost-effective?

options.A: Run claude code interactively, processing files one at a time with human oversight
options.B: Use the Batch API to submit all 500 conversions as a batch job with 50% cost savings
options.C: Spin up 500 parallel Claude Code sessions, one per file, for maximum speed
options.D: Write a traditional script to do the YAML-to-TOML conversion without using Claude

explanations.A: WRONG — Interactive processing of 500 files is extremely slow and wasteful of human time. This is a perfect automation candidate.
explanations.B: CORRECT — The Batch API is designed for exactly this: large volumes of independent tasks where latency is not critical. It offers 50% cost savings over real-time API calls and handles queuing, retries, and result collection automatically. Results are available within 24 hours.
explanations.C: WRONG — 500 parallel sessions would work but at full price. Since the results aren't needed urgently, the Batch API's 50% discount makes it far more cost-effective.
explanations.D: PARTIALLY CORRECT — A traditional script might work for simple format conversion, but it won't handle edge cases (comments, complex nested structures, semantic preservation) as well as an LLM. If the conversion is truly mechanical, this could be valid, but the question asks about Claude-based strategies.

questions.question: You need to find all TypeScript files in a large monorepo that contain the string 'deprecated'. Which combination of Claude Code built-in tools is most efficient?

options.A: Use Bash to run 'find . -name "*.ts" | xargs grep deprecated'
options.B: Use Read on every .ts file and search the content manually
options.C: Use Grep with pattern 'deprecated' and glob '*.ts' to search file contents directly
options.D: Use Glob to find all .ts files, then use Read on each one to check for 'deprecated'

explanations.A: WRONG — While this works, Claude Code's built-in Grep tool is optimized for this exact use case. Using Bash for search bypasses the built-in tool's optimizations (permissions, output formatting, result limits).
explanations.B: WRONG — Reading every file is extremely slow and wasteful. A monorepo may have thousands of .ts files. This is O(n) file reads vs a single Grep call.
explanations.C: CORRECT — Grep is the purpose-built tool for content search. Setting pattern to 'deprecated' and glob to '*.ts' performs the search in a single optimized call. It handles permissions, large repos, and output formatting automatically.
explanations.D: WRONG — Glob finds files by name pattern, not content. Using Glob + Read is a two-step process that requires reading every file. Grep does both steps in one call.

questions.question: A developer adds the following to the project's CLAUDE.md (committed to the shared repo): 'Always use vim keybindings. Dark theme preferred. Sign commits with my GPG key ABC123.' What is wrong with this?

options.A: Nothing — CLAUDE.md is the right place for all Claude Code configuration
options.B: The GPG key is a security risk, but the other preferences are fine in project CLAUDE.md
options.C: Personal preferences (vim, dark theme, personal GPG key) belong in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, not the shared project CLAUDE.md. Anti-Pattern #10.
options.D: These settings should be in .claude/settings.json, not CLAUDE.md

explanations.A: WRONG — Project CLAUDE.md is for PROJECT conventions (coding style, architecture decisions, team workflows), not individual preferences. Other team members may prefer different editors and themes.
explanations.B: WRONG — The GPG key IS a concern, but ALL three items are personal preferences. Vim keybindings and dark theme are individual choices that shouldn't be imposed on the team.
explanations.C: CORRECT — Anti-Pattern #10: personal preferences in project CLAUDE.md. The cascade hierarchy exists precisely for this: personal preferences go in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level, not committed). Project CLAUDE.md should contain only team-wide conventions.
explanations.D: WRONG — settings.json handles tool permissions and security settings, not coding preferences. The issue is which CLAUDE.md level these preferences belong in.

questions.question: You are building a pipeline step where Claude must ALWAYS call a validation tool before responding to the user. The tool is called 'validate_output'. Which tool_choice configuration ensures this behavior?

options.A: tool_choice: {type: 'auto'} — the model will figure out it needs to validate
options.B: tool_choice: {type: 'any'} — forces the model to use some tool, which will likely be validate_output
options.C: tool_choice: {type: 'tool', name: 'validate_output'} — forces the model to call this specific tool
options.D: Add 'You MUST call validate_output before responding' to the system prompt

explanations.A: WRONG — 'auto' lets the model decide whether to use tools at all. It might skip validation entirely if it feels confident in its output.
explanations.B: WRONG — 'any' forces tool use but doesn't guarantee WHICH tool. If multiple tools are available, the model might call a different one.
explanations.C: CORRECT — tool_choice: {type: 'tool', name: 'validate_output'} deterministically forces the model to call the specified tool. This is the only option that guarantees the validation step runs. Use this for mandatory pipeline steps.
explanations.D: WRONG — Prompt-based enforcement is probabilistic (Anti-Pattern #3). The model might skip the validation call, especially under complex contexts. tool_choice provides deterministic enforcement.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline uses Claude to validate Terraform configurations. When validation fails, the model returns: 'The configuration has errors. Please fix and retry.' This message is unhelpful. What is the correct validation-retry loop design?

options.A: Add 'Be more specific about errors' to the system prompt
options.B: Return the full Terraform error log to Claude and let it parse the relevant parts
options.C: Implement a structured retry loop: (1) run terraform validate, (2) parse SPECIFIC errors with line numbers, (3) feed errors back to Claude with the original code, (4) request targeted fixes, (5) re-validate, (6) repeat up to max_retries
options.D: Skip Claude for validation — just run terraform validate directly

explanations.A: WRONG — 'Be more specific' is itself vague (ironic). The model needs STRUCTURED error information, not a vague instruction to be less vague. Anti-Pattern #13.
explanations.B: PARTIALLY CORRECT — Feeding error logs back is good, but dumping the FULL log without parsing is noisy. The model may fixate on warnings instead of errors, or miss the root cause buried in verbose output.
explanations.C: CORRECT — The validation-retry loop pattern requires: specific error extraction (not raw logs), targeted feedback (line numbers, error codes), structured re-prompting (original code + specific errors), and bounded retries (max_retries prevents infinite loops). This is the proven CI/CD integration pattern.
explanations.D: WRONG — terraform validate alone can't fix the issues. The question asks about the validation-retry LOOP, which uses Claude to interpret errors and generate fixes.

questions.question: A developer writes the following prompt for a code review agent: 'Review this code and make it better.' The agent's reviews are inconsistent — sometimes it focuses on formatting, sometimes on logic, sometimes on performance. What anti-pattern is this and how do you fix it?

options.A: Add more examples of good reviews to the prompt (few-shot learning)
options.B: This is Anti-Pattern #13 (vague instructions). Fix: specify exact review criteria — 'Check for: (1) null pointer risks, (2) SQL injection, (3) missing error handling, (4) functions > 50 lines. Rate each: pass/warn/fail with line numbers.'
options.C: Increase temperature to make the model more creative in finding issues
options.D: Run the review three times and combine the results for comprehensive coverage

explanations.A: PARTIALLY CORRECT — Few-shot examples help, but they don't fix the root cause. Without explicit criteria, examples just shift WHICH inconsistency pattern the model follows.
explanations.B: CORRECT — Anti-Pattern #13: vague instructions yield inconsistent outputs. 'Make it better' gives the model no criteria for what 'better' means. The fix is explicit, enumerated criteria with specific thresholds and output format requirements. This makes reviews consistent and auditable.
explanations.C: WRONG — Higher temperature increases randomness, making inconsistency WORSE. The problem isn't creativity — it's lack of direction.
explanations.D: WRONG — Running three times triples cost without addressing the root cause. Each run will focus on different random aspects, and combining them doesn't ensure completeness.
